title: Where Am I?
Positional Encoding
en.hv1: Haviv et al. 2022, Findings of EMNLP:
en.addS: the same length as the word vector
en.pairS: slot 2i: sine · slot 2i+1: cosine · the same angle
en.ow: one word later: the hand turns
en.qT: why a sine AND a cosine?
en.rS: each hand by its own fixed angle; it depends only on k
en.pf2: sine and cosine of a sum mix: a turn
en.ruS: her rule: try a multiplication, or a concatenation

cap.n0: The cat chased the dog.|The dog chased the cat.
cap.n1: To attention with no positions,|these two are the same sentence.|So how does a Transformer know where each word sits?
cap.n2: In the 2017 Transformer,|the encoder lets every word look at every other word,|all at once.
cap.c2: In that scenario, if you look at these two sentences,|they will be the same
cap.n3: Each word mixes in the others by how well they match.|Nothing in that mix says which word came first.
cap.n4: Shake the words into a bag:|the, cat, chased, the, dog.|Both sentences give the same bag,|and the same result for every word.
cap.n5: Her slide says it plainly:|without positional encoding,|you cannot tell these two apart.
cap.n6: One honest footnote. In a decoder-only model,|each word sees only the words before it,|so the two sentences already look different.
cap.n7: A 2022 paper by Haviv and colleagues found that such models,|with no positional encoding at all,|still learn word order and come close to the usual ones.|Encoders that see both ways do not.
cap.n8: Positional encoding is still the standard.|So what does it look like?
cap.n9: The 2017 answer: give every position a vector,|the same length as a word's vector,|and add the two together.
cap.n10: And that vector is not learned.|It is computed from just two numbers:|the position, and the slot.
cap.c3: It's not a weight matrix.|You do not need to train it.
cap.n11: Here is the trick. Take the slots in pairs.|The first gets a sine,|the second a cosine, of the same angle.
cap.c4: But they always have the same angles for each two pieces.
cap.n12: A sine and a cosine of one angle|are just the tip of a clock hand,|on a circle of radius one.
cap.n13: So each pair of slots is one clock hand.|Move one word later, and the hand turns.
cap.n14: Her example uses eight slots, so four hands.
cap.n15: The first hand turns one radian per word, about 57 degrees.
cap.n16: The next turns 0.1 of a radian, then 0.01, then 0.001.|The slowest hand barely moves.
cap.n17: Read all four hands together,|and the positions are told apart.
cap.n18: Her slide 26 prints the readings.|Position 1, slot 0: 0.841471, the sine of one radian.
cap.n19: Down in slot 6, the slow hand reads 0.001.|Fast at the top, slow at the bottom.
cap.n20: Every value stays between minus one and one,|and there are no extra parameters.
cap.c5: If you can ensure your values are healthy,|it will make your model much more stable.
cap.n21: Why so many speeds? Fast hands tell neighbours apart.|Slow hands tell near from far, across a whole text.
cap.n22: In the 512-wide model,|the fastest hand comes round every 6.28 words.|The slowest takes about 60,000.
cap.n23: Now the clever part.|Why a sine and a cosine, and not just a sine?
cap.n24: Think of a question you ask after|pasting in a long document.
cap.c8: after you have a PDF, you ask a question.
cap.n25: Every word of the question moves|later by the document's length.|Its meaning should not change.
cap.n26: Moving every word k places later turns|each hand by its own fixed angle.|That is a rotation, and it depends only on k,|not on where you started.
cap.n27: Turn two hands by the same angle,|and the angle between them stays put.
cap.n28: So the dot product of two position vectors,|a score of how much two arrows point the same way,|depends only on how far apart the words are.
cap.n29: Her slide 27 writes it as:|P E of pos plus k equals R k times P E of pos.|Rotate both, and the dot product is unchanged.
cap.n30: The proof is on her next slides, as self-study.
cap.n31: The short version:|the sine and cosine of a sum of angles mix into each other,|exactly like a turning hand.
cap.n32: So, problem solved? Not quite.|Remember, the position is added to the word.
cap.n33: Like two jars poured into one glass,|the word and its clock reading become a single vector.
cap.c10: But how about the entire part? No, it's not.
cap.n34: Attention compares those mixed vectors.|The position-with-position part keeps the distance,|but the word-with-position parts|change when both words move.
cap.n35: Her slide 31: How at position 1 with You at position 3 does|not score the same as How at 2 with You at 4,|even though the gap is the same.
cap.n36: The relative distance is only partly there.
cap.n37: Her rule of thumb: when you see an addition,|ask whether a multiplication or|a concatenation would do better.
cap.n38: Multiply instead, and you get RoPE,|from Su and colleagues in 2021.|It turns the query and the key themselves.|That is the next episode.
cap.n39: Clock hands at many speeds give every word its place.|Added to the word, they keep the distance only partly.|Next time: turn, don't add.
